blocks.html:
Exposé XV
ACYCLIC MORPHISMSby M. Artin
Contents

1. Generalities on globally and locally acyclic morphisms
2. Local acyclicity of a smooth morphism
3. Proof of the main lemma
4. Appendix: A criterion for local \(0\)-acyclicity
Introduction

Let \(g : X \to Y\) be a morphism of schemes. In the first section, we study conditions for \(g\) to be acyclic, that is, such that for every torsion sheaf \(F\) on \(Y\) one has \(H^q(Y,F) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^q(X, g^* F)\), and such that this remains true if one replaces \(Y\) by a \(Y'\) étale over \(Y\). A natural necessary condition for acyclicity is that the geometric fibres be acyclic, that is, have trivial cohomology for constant torsion sheaves. We shall see that this condition, together with a local condition, called local acyclicity of \(f\) (1.11), implies that \(f\) is acyclic.

The fundamental theorem is that a smooth morphism is locally acyclic for torsion sheaves prime to the residue characteristics (2.1); this will imply the base change theorem for a smooth morphism (XVI 1.1), which will be developed, together with its first consequences, in the following exposé.

The present exposé is independent of exposés XI to XIV, and in particular of the "base change theorem for a proper morphism". The latter will again intervene in an essential way, but in conjunction with the fundamental theorem of the present exposé, starting from the following exposé.

pages.title: 1. Generalities on globally and locally acyclic morphisms.

blocks.html: 1. Generalities on globally and locally acyclic morphisms.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.1

Let \(g : X \to Y\) be a morphism of schemes. The following assertions (i) to (iii) are equivalent:

(i) For each \(Y' \to Y\) étale (which one may take affine over an affine open set of \(Y\)) and each sheaf of sets \(F\) on \(Y'\), the canonical morphism \(F \to g'_* g'^* F\) is injective (resp. bijective).

(ii) For each \(Y' \to Y\) étale (which one may take affine over an affine open set of \(Y\)) and each sheaf of sets \(F\) on \(Y'\), the canonical morphism \(H^0(Y',F) \to H^0(X',g'^* F)\) is injective (resp. bijective).

(iii) For each \(Y' \to Y\) locally quasi-finite and each sheaf of sets \(F\) on \(Y'\), the canonical morphism \(H^0(Y',F) \to H^0(X',g'^* F)\) is injective (resp. bijective).

(ii bis) (If \(f\) is quasi-compact and quasi-separated). As (ii), but taking \(F\) a constant sheaf of the form \(I_{Y'}\), where \(I\) is a set given in advance, with \(\operatorname{card} I \geqslant 2\).

Proof. The equivalence of (i) and (ii) is immediate from the definitions, and (iii) \(\Longrightarrow\) (ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) (ii bis) are trivial. We have (ii bis) \(\Longrightarrow\) (ii), for one may assume \(Y\) affine, hence \(X\) and \(Y\) quasi-compact and quasi-separated, and one may then apply XII 6.5 (i). For the implication (i) \(\Longrightarrow\) (iii), let us first note the following lemma:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.2

Let \(f : Y' \to Y\) be a locally quasi-finite morphism. Then \(f\) is "finite locally on \(Y'\) for the étale topology", that is, one has commutative diagrams

\[(*)\qquad \xymatrix{ Y_i' \ar[r]^{a_i} \ar[d]_{b_i} & Y' \ar[d]^{f} \\ Y_i \ar[r]_{c_i} & Y }\]

where the \(a_i\), \(c_i\) are étale, the \(b_i\) are finite, and the \(a_i\) form a covering of \(Y'\) (∗).

Indeed, let \(y'\) be a point of \(Y'\) and \(y = f(y')\). It suffices to find a diagram \((*)\) such that \(y'\) lies in the image of \(Y_i'\). Let \(\widetilde{Y}\) be the spectrum of the henselization of the ring \(\mathcal{O}_{Y,y}\) (VIII 4.1) and \(Z\) the (ordinary) localization of \(\widetilde{Y}' = Y' \times_Y \widetilde{Y}\) at the unique point lying over \(y'\) and over the closed point \(\mathring{y}\) of \(\widetilde{Y}\). By VIII 4.1 (ii), \(Z \to \widetilde{Y}\) is finite, and \(Z\) is an open subset of \(\widetilde{Y}'\). Since \(\widetilde{Y}\) is a limit of preschemes \(Y_i\) étale over \(Y\), one sees at once (EGA IV 9) that for suitable \(Y_i\) there exists an open set \(Z_i\) of \(Y' \times_Y Y_i\) such that \(Z = Z_i \times_{Y_i} \widetilde{Y}\), and in \((*)\) it will suffice to take \(Y_i' = Z_i\), q.e.d.

Suppose now that (i) of 1.1 holds. It is clear that assertion (iii) of 1.1 is equivalent to the assertion obtained from (i) by replacing the étale morphism \(Y' \to Y\) by a locally quasi-finite morphism. In this form, the assertion (for given \(Y\), \(Y'\)) is local on \(Y\) and \(Y'\) for the étale topology, and one is therefore reduced, by the lemma, to the case of a finite morphism \(f : Y' \to Y\). Let \(f' : X' \to X\) be the morphism deduced from \(f\) by the base change \(g\). Then the base change morphism \(g^* f_* F \to f'_* g'^* F\) is bijective (VIII 5.6). By (i), one has \(f_*(F) \to g_* g^* f_* F\). Consequently the morphism \(H^0(Y',F) \xrightarrow{\ \varepsilon\ } H^0(Y',g'_* g'^* F)\) of (iii) is the composite
\[H^0(Y',F) = H^0(Y,f_* F) \xrightarrow{\ \varepsilon'\ } H^0(Y, g_* g^* f_* F) = H^0(X, g^* f_* F) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^0(X, f'_* g'^* F) = H^0(X', g'^* F) \;.\]
Since \(\varepsilon'\) is injective (resp. bijective), so is \(\varepsilon\). This completes the proof of 1.1.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.3

A morphism \(g : X \to Y\) having one of the equivalent properties (i) to (iii) (resp. (i) to (iii) in the resp. sense) of 1.1 is called a \((-1)\)-acyclic (resp. \(0\)-acyclic) morphism. The morphism is said to be universally \((-1)\)-acyclic (resp. \(0\)-acyclic) if for each base change morphism \(Y' \to Y\), the morphism \(g' = g \times_Y Y' : X \times_Y Y' \to Y'\) is \((-1)\)-acyclic (resp. \(0\)-acyclic). Finally, a prescheme \(X\) is said to be \((-1)\)-acyclic (resp. \(0\)-acyclic) if it is non-empty (resp. connected and non-empty).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.4

Let \(g : X \to Y\) be a \(0\)-acyclic morphism. Then for each \(Y' \to Y\) locally quasi-finite and each sheaf of groups \(F\) on \(Y'\), the canonical morphism

\[H^1(Y',F) \to H^1(X',g'^* F)\]

is injective.
This follows at once from XII 6.5 (i).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.5

Let \(g : X \to Y\) be a morphism. If \(g\) is surjective (i.e. its fibres are non-empty, i.e. its fibres are \((-1)\)-acyclic) then \(g\) is \((-1)\)-acyclic. The converse is true if \(g\) is quasi-compact and quasi-separated.

The first assertion is evident in the form 1.1 (ii) by considering the fibres of the sheaves in question. The second follows from the definition in the form 1.1 (iii) and from the sorites for passage to the limit (VII 5), taking into account that for every \(y \in Y\), \(y = \operatorname{Spec} k(y)\) is a projective limit of affine schemes locally quasi-finite over \(Y\), namely the affine neighbourhoods of \(y\) in \(\overline{\{y\}}\) (endowed with the induced reduced structure). — Note that 1.5 implies that when \(g\) is quasi-compact and quasi-separated, then \(g\) \((-1)\)-acyclic already implies \(g\) universally \((-1)\)-acyclic.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.6

Let \(g : X \to Y\) be a morphism of schemes, \(\mathbb{L} \subset \mathbb{P}\) a set of prime numbers, and \(n \in \mathbb{N}\) a natural integer (resp. \(n = 1\)). The following assertions (i) to (iii) (resp. assertions (i) to (iii) in the resp. sense) are equivalent. If moreover \(g\) is quasi-compact and quasi-separated, then (i) to (iii) (resp. (i) to (iii) in the resp. sense) are also equivalent to (iv) (resp. (iv) in the resp. sense).

(i) For each \(Y' \to Y\) étale and each abelian sheaf of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion (resp. of ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-groups) (IX 1.5) \(F\) on \(Y'\), one has \[\begin{cases} F \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } g'_* g'^* F \;, \\ (R^q g'_*) g'^* F = 0 & \text{if } 1 \leqslant q \leqslant n \ (\text{resp. if } q = 1). \end{cases}\]

(ii) For each \(Y' \to Y\) étale and each abelian sheaf of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion (resp. of ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-groups) \(F\) on \(Y'\), the canonical morphism \[H^q(Y',F) \to H^q(X',g'^* F)\] is bijective if \(q \leqslant n\) and injective if \(q = n+1\) (resp. is bijective if \(q \leqslant 1\)).

(iii) For each \(Y' \to Y\) locally quasi-finite and each abelian sheaf of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion (resp. of ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-groups) \(F\) on \(Y'\), the morphism \[H^q(Y',F) \to H^q(X',g'^* F)\] is bijective if \(q \leqslant n\) and injective if \(q = n+1\) (resp. is bijective if \(q \leqslant 1\)).

(iv) The morphism \(g\) is surjective, and for each \(Y' \to Y\) locally quasi-finite, each \(\nu > 0\), and each \(\ell \in \mathbb{L}\), the canonical morphism \[H^q(Y', \mathbb{Z}/\ell^\nu) \to H^q(X', \mathbb{Z}/\ell^\nu)\] is surjective for \(0 \leqslant q \leqslant n\) (resp. for each \(Y' \to Y\) locally quasi-finite and each ordinary finite \(\mathbb{L}\)-group \(G\), the canonical morphism \[H^i(Y',G) \to H^i(X',G)\] is surjective for \(i = 0,1\)).

Proof of 1.6. The implications (ii) \(\Longleftarrow\) (iii) \(\Longrightarrow\) (iv) are trivial. Now \((R^q g'_*) g'^* F\) is the sheaf associated to the presheaf \(R^q(Y'') = H^q(X'', g''^* F)\) (\(Y'' \to Y'\) étale). If (ii) holds, one has \(H^q(Y'',F) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^q(X'',g''^* F)\), so the associated sheaf is zero, i.e. (ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) (i). The implication (i) \(\Longrightarrow\) (ii) follows from 1.1 (i) (which corresponds to the case \(n = 0\)) together with the Leray spectral sequence
\[H^p(Y', (R^q g'_*) g'^* F) \Longrightarrow H^{p+q}(X', g'^* F)\]
in the abelian case, and with the exact sequence
in the case of sheaves of groups.

(i) \(\Longrightarrow\) (iii): Since (i) and (ii) are equivalent, it is clear that (iii) is equivalent to the statement obtained from (i) by replacing the word "étale" by the words "locally quasi-finite". In this form it is, for given \(Y\), \(Y'\), an assertion local on \(Y'\) and on \(Y\) for the étale topology, and one is therefore reduced by 1.2 to the case where \(f : Y' \to Y\) is a finite morphism. Let \(f' : X' \to X\) be the morphism. By VIII 5.5 (resp. VIII 5.8) (applied three times) one has
\[f_*(R^q g'_*) g'^* F \simeq R^q(f g')_* g'^* F \simeq R^q(g f')_* g'^* F \simeq (R^q g_*) f'_* g'^* F \simeq (R^q g_*) g^*(f_* F)\]
and the latter is zero if (i) holds for the values of \(q\) under consideration, whence (i) \(\Longrightarrow\) (iii).
It remains to prove (iv) \(\Longrightarrow\) (iii); now this follows at once from XII 6.5.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.7

Let \(n \in \mathbb{N}\) and \(\mathbb{L} \subset \mathbb{P}\). A morphism \(g : X \to Y\) satisfying one of the equivalent conditions (i) to (iii) (resp. (i) to (iii) in the resp. sense) of 1.6 is called an \(n\)-acyclic morphism (resp. a \(1\)-aspherical morphism) for \(\mathbb{L}\). One says that \(g\) is acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\) if it is \(n\)-acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\) for every \(n\). One says that \(g\) is universally \(n\)-acyclic (resp. universally \(1\)-aspherical) for \(\mathbb{L}\) if for each \(Y' \to Y\) the morphism \(g' = g \times_Y Y'\) is \(n\)-acyclic (resp. \(1\)-aspherical) for \(\mathbb{L}\). Finally, a prescheme \(X\) is said to be \(n\)-acyclic (resp. \(1\)-aspherical) for \(\mathbb{L}\) if it is \(0\)-acyclic (1.3) and if for each \(\ell \in \mathbb{L}\) and each \(1 \leqslant q \leqslant n\) one has \(H^q(X, \mathbb{Z}/\ell) = 0\) (resp. and for each ordinary finite \(\mathbb{L}\)-group \(G\), one has \(H^1(X,G) = 0\)).

blocks.title: Remarks
blocks.html:
Remarks 1.8

a) If \(g\) is quasi-compact and quasi-separated, then in order for \(g\) to be universally \(n\)-acyclic it suffices that \(g'\) be \(n\)-acyclic whenever \(Y' \to Y\) is locally of finite presentation. We do not need this fact and leave its proof, which is an exercise in passage to the limit, to the reader.

b) We do not know whether a morphism that is \(n\)-acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\) is already universally \(n\)-acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\). The same question arises for the local variants below (1.11).

c) When \(n = 0\), one recovers the notion of 1.3. Of course, one could have written 1.6 and 1.7 so as to include the case \(n = -1\). The proposition that follows is also valid in this case.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.9

(i) Let \(X \xrightarrow{g} Y \xrightarrow{h} Z\) be morphisms of schemes, \(\mathbb{L} \subset \mathbb{P}\), and \(n \in \mathbb{N}\). Suppose that \(g\) is \(0\)-acyclic (resp. \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\), resp. \(n\)-acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\)). Let \(f = hg\). Then for every sheaf of sets (resp. of ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-groups, resp. abelian of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion) \(F\) on \(Z\), one has an isomorphism \(f_* f^* F \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } h_* h^* F\) (resp. isomorphisms \((R^p f_*) f^* F \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } (R^p h_*) h^* F\) if \(p \leqslant 1\), resp. if \(p \leqslant n\)). In particular, \(h\) is \(0\)-acyclic (resp. \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\), resp. \(n\)-acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\)) if and only if \(f\) is.

(ii) Let \(\{g_\alpha : X_\alpha \to Y_\alpha\}\) be a projective system of morphisms of schemes such that the morphisms \(X_\alpha \to X_\beta\) and \(Y_\alpha \to Y_\beta\) are affine and the \(g_\alpha\) are quasi-compact and quasi-separated. Let \(g : X \to Y\) be the projective limit of the \(g_\alpha\) (VII 5.1). Then if all the \(g_\alpha\) are \(0\)-acyclic (resp. \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\), resp. \(n\)-acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\)), so is \(g\).
Proof. For (i), one has first
\[h_* h^* F \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } h_*(g_* g^*) h^* F \simeq f_* f^* F \;.\]
The second assertion of (i) is an immediate consequence of the Leray spectral sequence
\[(R^p h_*)(R^q g_*) f^* F \Longrightarrow (R^{p+q} f_*) f^* F \;.\]
Finally, the non-abelian assertion follows from the exact sequence XII 3.2.
Assertion (ii) follows easily from the theory of passage to the limit (VII 5 and VI).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.9.1

Let \(g : X \to Y\) be a quasi-compact and quasi-separated morphism, and \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), \(\mathbb{L} \subset \mathbb{P}\). If \(g\) is \(n\)-acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\) (resp. \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\)), then for every geometric point \(\bar{y}\) of \(Y\), algebraic over a point \(y\) of \(Y\), the geometric fibre \(X_{\bar{y}}\) is \(n\)-acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\) (resp. \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\)).

Indeed, \(\bar{y}\) is a projective limit of affine schemes \(Y_i\) that are locally quasi-finite over \(Y\), and since the \(X_i = X \times_Y Y_i \to Y_i\) are \(n\)-acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\) (resp. ...), so is \(X_{\bar{y}} \to \bar{y}\) by virtue of 1.9 (ii), whence the announced conclusion.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.10

Let \(g : X \to Y\) be a morphism of schemes, \(\mathbb{L} \subset \mathbb{P}\), and \(n \in \mathbb{N}\). Then the following conditions (i) to (iv) are equivalent.

(i) Let \(\bar{y}\) be a geometric point of \(Y\) and \(\bar{x}\) a geometric point of \(X\) lying over \(\bar{y}\). Let \(\widetilde{X}\), \(\widetilde{Y}\) be the strict localizations of \(X\), \(Y\) at the points \(\bar{x}\), \(\bar{y}\), and let \(\widehat{g} : \widetilde{X} \to \widetilde{Y}\) be the morphism induced by \(g\). Then \(\widehat{g}\) is \(0\)-acyclic (resp. \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\), resp. \(n\)-acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\)).

(ii) For each diagram with cartesian squares \[(*)\qquad \xymatrix{ X \ar[d]_{g} & X' \ar[l]_{j} \ar[d]_{g'} & X'' \ar[l]_{j'} \ar[d]^{g''} \\ Y & Y' \ar[l]^{i} & Y'' \ar[l]^{i'} }\] with \(i\) étale and \(i'\) étale of finite presentation, and each sheaf of sets (resp. of ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-groups, resp. abelian of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion) \(F\) on \(Y''\), the base change morphism (XII 4.1, 4.2) \[g'^* i'_* F \to j'_* g''^* F\] is bijective (resp. the morphisms \[g'^*(R^q i'_*)F \to (R^q j'_*) g''^* F\] are bijective for \(q = 0, 1\), resp. are bijective for \(0 \leqslant q \leqslant n\) and injective for \(q = n+1\)).

(iii) Same statement as (ii), except that the morphism \(i'\) is assumed only quasi-finite and quasi-separated.

(iv) Same statement as (ii), but assuming \(i\) only locally quasi-finite, and on the other hand \(i'\) a quasi-compact open immersion.

Proof. The implication (iii) \(\Longrightarrow\) (ii) is trivial. Let us verify that (i) \(\Longrightarrow\) (iii). It suffices to examine the morphism of (iii) fibre by fibre. Let \(\bar{y}\) be a geometric point of \(Y'\) and \(\bar{x}\) a geometric point of \(X'\) lying over \(\bar{y}\). Let
\[\xymatrix{ \widetilde{X}' \ar[d]_{\widetilde{g}'} & \widetilde{X}'' \ar[l]_{\widetilde{j}'} \ar[d]^{\widetilde{g}''} \\ \widetilde{Y}' & \widehat{Y}'' \ar[l]^{\widetilde{i}'} }\]

be the cartesian diagram deduced from \((*)\), where \(\widetilde{X}'\), \(\widetilde{Y}'\) are the strict localizations of \(X'\), \(Y'\) at the points \(\bar{x}\), \(\bar{y}\) and where \(\widehat{Y}'' = Y'' \times_{Y'} \widetilde{Y}'\), \(\widetilde{X}'' = X'' \times_{X'} \widetilde{X}'\). One has, by VIII 5.2 and 5.3,
\[H^q(\widehat{Y}'', \widehat{F}) \simeq (R^q i'_* F)_{\bar{y}} \simeq (g'^*(R^q i'_* F))_{\bar{x}} \;,\]
where \(\widehat{F}\) is the inverse image of \(F\) on \(\widehat{Y}''\), and
\[H^q(\widetilde{X}'', \widetilde{g}''^* \widehat{F}) \simeq ((R^q j'_*) g''^* F)_{\bar{x}} \;.\]
Since \(\widetilde{i}'\) is quasi-finite, one may apply 1.1 (iii) (resp. 1.5 (iii)) to the morphism
\[H^q(\widehat{Y}'', \widehat{F}) \to H^q(\widetilde{X}'', \widetilde{g}''^* \widehat{F})\]
for the values of \(q\) under consideration, whence (i) \(\Longrightarrow\) (iii).

(ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) (i). Suppose (ii) holds and let us verify the acyclicity criterion 1.6 (ii) for a morphism \(\widetilde{g} : \widetilde{X} \to \widetilde{Y}\). Let \(\widehat{Y}' \to \widetilde{Y}\) be étale, with \(\widehat{Y}'\) affine, and let \(\widehat{F}\) be a sheaf of sets (resp. abelian of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion, resp. of ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-groups) on \(\widehat{Y}'\). One must prove that
\[H^q(\widehat{Y}', \widehat{F}) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^q(\widetilde{X}', \widetilde{g}'^* \widehat{F}) \;,\]

where \(\widetilde{g}' : \widetilde{X}' \to \widehat{Y}'\) is the morphism deduced from \(\widetilde{g}\) by base change. Now let us write \(\widetilde{Y} = \varprojlim Y_\alpha\) where the \(Y_\alpha\) are étale and affine over \(Y\) (assuming \(Y\) affine, which is permissible). One may "descend" the étale morphism \(\widehat{Y}' \to \widetilde{Y}\) to one of the \(Y_\alpha\), say to \(Y'_o \to Y_o\), and one has \(\widehat{Y}' = \varprojlim Y'_\alpha = \widetilde{Y} \times_{Y_o} Y'_o\). Now each sheaf \(\widehat{F}\) on \(\widehat{Y}'\) is the inductive limit of the sheaves \(f'^*_\alpha f'_{\alpha *} \widehat{F}\), where \(f'_\alpha : Y'_\alpha \to Y'_o\) is the canonical morphism. By XII 1.2 (v) and 1.6 (iii) the sheaves \(f'_{\alpha *} \widehat{F}\) are sheaves of sets (resp. abelian of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion, resp. of ind-\(\mathbb{L}\)-groups). Taking VII 3.3 into account, one sees therefore that it suffices to treat the case where \(\widehat{F}\) descends to one of the \(Y'_\alpha\), say to an \(F_o\) on \(Y'_o\). Applying (ii) to the diagram
\[\xymatrix{ X \ar[d]_{g} & X_o \ar[l] \ar[d]_{g_o} & X'_o \ar[l]_{j'_o} \ar[d]^{g'_o} \\ Y & Y_o \ar[l] & Y'_o \ar[l]^{i'_o} }\]

one deduces that \(g_o^*(R^q i'_{o*})F_o \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } (R^q j'_{o*}) g_o'^* F_o\) for the applicable values of \(q\). Now the geometric points \(\bar{y}\), \(\bar{x}\) lift canonically to geometric points of \(Y_o\), \(X_o\) (which we denote by the same symbols), and one has, by VIII 5.2 and 5.3,
\[H^q(\widehat{Y}', \widehat{F}) = ((R^q i'_{o*})F_o)_{\bar{y}} = (g_o^*(R^q i'_{o*})F_o)_{\bar{x}}\]
and
\[H^q(\widetilde{X}', \widetilde{g}'^* \widehat{F}) = ((R^q j'_{o*}) g_o'^* F_o)_{\bar{x}}\]
for the values of \(q\) under consideration, whence the result.

It remains to show that conditions (i) to (iii) are equivalent to (iv). Now, using form (i), one sees that these conditions are stable under locally quasi-finite base extension \(Y' \to Y\), from which it follows at once, in form (ii), that they imply (iv). On the other hand, (iv) implies (iii), for in order to verify (iii) one sees immediately, using for example the Leray spectral sequence, or the descent result XII 6.8, that one may assume \(Y'\) and \(Y''\) affine. But then by the "Main Theorem" EGA IV 8.12.7 \(Y'' \to Y'\) factors as \(Y'' \xrightarrow{i'_1} Y'_1 \xrightarrow{i'_2} Y'\), with \(i'_1\) an open immersion and \(i'_2\) a finite morphism. Using VIII 5.5, 5.8 for \(i'_2\), one is reduced to verifying (ii) for \(i'_1\), which comes under (iv). This completes the proof of 1.10.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.11

A morphism \(g : X \to Y\) of preschemes satisfying one of the equivalent conditions (i) to (iv) of 1.10 is called a locally \(0\)-acyclic morphism (resp. locally \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\), resp. locally \(n\)-acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\)). One defines in an obvious way (compare 1.7) the notions of locally acyclic morphism, and of universally locally \(0\)-acyclic (resp. ...) morphism for \(\mathbb{L}\).

One may naturally vary statements (i) to (iii) of 1.10. Thus, in (iii) and (iv) one may confine oneself to a constant sheaf \(F\) of the form \(G_I\), \(G\) a finite set (resp. a finite \(\mathbb{L}\)-group, resp. \(G\) of the form \(\mathbb{Z}/\ell^\nu \mathbb{Z}\), with \(\ell \in \mathbb{L}\), \(\nu \in \mathbb{N}\)); this follows easily from VIII 5.2, 5.3 and from XII 6.5. Let us also point out the following variant:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.12

Suppose \(g : X \to Y\) locally of finite type. To verify local \(0\)-acyclicity (resp. ...), it suffices to verify 1.10 (i) in the case where the geometric point \(\bar{x}\) is closed in the geometric fibre \(X_{\bar{y}}\).

Indeed, in the proof of (i) \(\Longrightarrow\) (iii) of 1.10, one verified (iii) fibre by fibre, and it sufficed to do so for the fibres at the geometric points \(\bar{x}\) that are closed in their geometric fibre, since \(g\) is locally of finite type (VIII 3.13 b).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.13

(i) Let \(X \xrightarrow{g} Y \xrightarrow{h} Z\) be morphisms of schemes, \(\mathbb{L} \subset \mathbb{P}\), and \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), and suppose that \(g\) is surjective, and locally \(0\)-acyclic (resp. locally \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\), resp. locally \(n\)-acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\)). Then \(h\) is locally \(0\)-acyclic (resp. ...) if and only if \(f = hg\) is.

(ii) Let \(\{g_\alpha : X_\alpha \to Y_\alpha\}\) be a projective system of morphisms of preschemes such that the morphisms \(X_\alpha \to X_\beta\) and \(Y_\alpha \to Y_\beta\) are affine. Let \(g\) be the projective limit of the \(\{g_\alpha\}\) (VII 5.1). Then if all the \(g_\alpha\) are locally \(0\)-acyclic (resp. ...), so is \(g\).
This is a sorites analogous to 1.9.

blocks.title: Remarks
blocks.html:
Remarks 1.14

To simplify his task, the writer has omitted, in 1.10 to 1.13, to treat also the case \(n = -1\), and he leaves it to the reader to convince himself that the statements, definitions and proofs apply essentially without change to this case. Thus, with the notation of 1.10, condition (i) is expressed by saying that the local induced morphisms \(\widetilde{X} \to \widetilde{Y}\) are \((-1)\)-acyclic, i.e. by 1.5 surjective, and conditions (ii) to (iv) are expressed by saying that the base change morphism \(g'^*(i'_*(F)) \to j'_*(g''^*(F))\) is a monomorphism. Under these conditions, one will therefore say that \(g\) is locally \((-1)\)-acyclic. This condition is thus stable under locally quasi-finite base extension. As an example, let us point out that a flat morphism is locally \((-1)\)-acyclic, for such a morphism the surjectivity condition for the \(\widetilde{X} \to \widetilde{Y}\) is a well-known consequence of the flatness of these morphisms. On the other hand, let us also point out that when \(f\) is locally of finite presentation, then \(f\) is locally \((-1)\)-acyclic if and only if it is universally open, at least when \(Y\) is locally noetherian: this indeed follows easily from EGA IV 14.4.9, 1.10.3. For such a morphism, local \((-1)\)-acyclicity consequently implies universal local \((-1)\)-acyclicity. (It is moreover very probable (∗) that in these last statements the locally noetherian hypothesis on \(Y\) is unnecessary: this is in any case so if the set of irreducible components of \(Y\) is locally finite (EGA IV 14.4.10)).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 1.15

Let \(g : X \to Y\) be a quasi-compact and quasi-separated morphism, \(\mathbb{L} \subset \mathbb{P}\) a set of prime numbers, \(n\) a natural integer (resp. \(n = 1\)). Suppose that \(g\) is \((n-1)\)-acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\) and locally \(n\)-acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\) (1.3, 1.7, 1.11, 1.14). Let \(F\) be a sheaf on \(Y\), which for \(n \geqslant 1\) is assumed to be endowed with a structure of abelian sheaf of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion (resp. with a structure of sheaf of groups), and let \(\xi\) be an element of \(H^n(X, g^*(F))\). In order for \(\xi\) to come from an element of \(H^n(Y,F)\) (which is then uniquely determined, thanks to the hypothesis of \((n-1)\)-acyclicity on \(g\)), it is necessary and sufficient that for every geometric point \(\bar{y}\) of \(Y\), algebraic over a point \(y\) of \(Y\), the image \(\xi_{\bar{y}}\) of \(\xi\) in \(H^n(X_{\bar{y}}, F | X_{\bar{y}})\) lie in the image of \(H^n(\bar{y}, F_{\bar{y}})\) (which, for \(n \geqslant 1\), means that one has \(\xi_{\bar{y}} = 0\)).

Let us note at once that one concludes from 1.15 that, under the preliminary conditions envisaged for \(g\), \(g\) is \(n\)-acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\) (resp. \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\)) if and only if for every \(\bar{y}\) as above, \(X_{\bar{y}}\) is \(n\)-acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\) (resp. is \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\)): the "if" indeed follows directly from 1.15 and the definitions, the "only if" being in any case immediate by 1.9.1. This said, an immediate induction on \(n\) yields the

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.16

Let \(g\) be a quasi-compact and quasi-separated morphism that is locally \((n-1)\)-acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\), where \(n\) is a given natural integer (resp. where \(n = 1\)). Then \(g\) is \(n\)-acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\) (resp. is \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\)) if and only if for every geometric point \(\bar{y}\) of \(Y\), algebraic over a point \(y\) of \(Y\), the fibre \(X_{\bar{y}}\) is \(n\)-acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\) (resp. \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\)).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.17

Let \(g : X \to Y\) be a morphism of preschemes, \(\mathbb{L} \subset \mathbb{P}\) a set of prime numbers, \(n\) a natural integer (resp. \(n = 1\)). In order for \(g\) to be locally \(n\)-acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\) (resp. locally \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\)), it is necessary and sufficient that for every geometric point \(\bar{x}\) of \(X\), if \(\widetilde{g} : \widetilde{X} \to \widetilde{Y}\) is the morphism of the strict localizations of \(X\) and \(Y\) (at \(\bar{x}\) and the corresponding geometric point \(\bar{y}\) of \(Y\)) induced by \(g\), each geometric fibre \(X_{\bar{z}}\) of \(\widetilde{g}\), relative to a geometric point \(\bar{z}\) of \(\widetilde{Y}\) algebraic over a point \(z\) of \(\widetilde{Y}\), is \(n\)-acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\) (resp. \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\)).

The necessity indeed follows from the criterion 1.10 (i) and from 1.9.1; for the sufficiency one proceeds by induction on \(n\), which allows us, when \(n \geqslant 1\), to assume that \(g\) is already locally \((n-1)\)-acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\). The morphisms \(\widetilde{g}\) then have the same property, and 1.16 then implies that \(\widetilde{g}\) is \(n\)-acyclic (resp. \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\)), which by virtue of the criterion 1.10 (i) implies that \(g\) is locally \(n\)-acyclic (resp. locally \(1\)-aspherical) for \(\mathbb{L}\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.18

With the notation of 1.17, if \(g\) is locally of finite type, then in the stated criterion one may confine oneself to taking geometric points \(\bar{x}\) whose locality \(x\) is closed in its fibre.
This indeed follows from the proof given and from 1.12.

Let \(\bar{y}\) be the geometric point corresponding to a separable closure of \(k(y)\), so that \(\bar{y}\) is a filtered projective limit of open sets \(U_i\) of finite integral schemes \(Y_i\) over \(Y\), each of which is such that its image in \(Y\) contains a neighbourhood of \(y\). Remark 1.18

One can give a refinement of 1.15, which provides a distinctly simpler proof of 1.15 when \(Y\) is assumed locally noetherian. For this, in addition to the preliminary hypotheses on \(g\), \(F\), suppose that there exists a finite number of geometric points \(f_i : \bar{y}_i \to Y\) of \(Y\) such that the morphism \[F \to \prod_i f_{i*}(f_i^*(F))\] is injective (a hypothesis automatically satisfied if \(Y\) is noetherian and if \(F\) is constructible IX 2.14).

I claim that under these conditions the criterion 1.15 is valid when one confines oneself to the geometric points \(\bar{y}_i\) alone. Indeed, by virtue of XII 6.6 one may assume that \(F\) is itself of the form \(f_*(M_{\bar{y}})\), where \(M\) is a set, resp. a group, resp. an abelian group of \(\mathbb{L}\)-torsion, and \(f : \bar{y} \to Y\) a geometric point. Let \(f' : X' = X_{\bar{y}} \to X\) be the canonical morphism. Assuming, to fix ideas, \(n \geqslant 1\), the local hypothesis made on \(g\) implies that one has
\[g^*(f_*(M_{\bar{y}})) \simeq f'_*(M_{X'}) \;, \qquad R^i f'_*(M_{X'}) = 0 \quad \text{for } 1 \leqslant i \leqslant n-1 \;,\]

the second relation coming from the fact that the first term is isomorphic to \(g^*(R^i f_*(M_{\bar{y}}))\), which is zero since manifestly \(R^i f_*(M_{\bar{y}}) = 0\) for \(i \geqslant 1\). From these relations, one concludes that

pages.title: 2. Local acyclicity of a smooth morphism.

blocks.html: 2. Local acyclicity of a smooth morphism.
The theorem is the following:

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 2.1

Let \(g : X \to Y\) be a smooth morphism and let \(\mathbb{L} \subset \mathbb{P}\) be the complement of the set of residue characteristics of \(X\). Then \(g\) is locally acyclic and locally \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\).
Let us first note the corollary:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.2

Let \(g : \mathbb{E}^m_Y \to Y\) be the structural morphism of affine space. Then \(g\) is acyclic and \(1\)-aspherical for the set \(\mathbb{L}\) complementary to the set of residue characteristics of \(Y\).

Indeed, by induction on \(m\) and by 1.9 (i) one reduces to the case \(m = 1\). By 2.1 one knows that \(g\) is locally \(n\)-acyclic and locally \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\), hence that the local condition of 1.16 is satisfied. It therefore suffices to prove that the geometric fibres of \(\mathbb{E}^1_Y\) are acyclic and \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\), that is, that \(\operatorname{Spec} k[t]\) is acyclic and \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\) if \(k\) is a separably closed field of characteristic \(p \notin \mathbb{L}\); this follows from IX 4.6 for the acyclicity assertion, and for the \(1\)-asphericity it is well known. More generally, let \(X'\) be an irreducible normal Galois covering of \(X = \mathbb{P}^1_k\), unramified outside the point \(\infty\) and whose ramification at that point is tame. Let us prove that the degree \(n\) of the covering is equal to \(1\). Now one has the Hurwitz formula:

where \(g\), \(g'\) are the genus of \(X\), \(X'\), and \(\mathfrak{D}_{X'/X}\) the different divisor. One has \(g = 0\), and the hypothesis of tame ramification implies \(\deg \mathfrak{D}_{X'/X} \leqslant n-1\), whence \(2(g'-1) \leqslant -(n+1)\), so \(n \leqslant 2(1-g')-1\), and since \(g' \geqslant 0\), one concludes \(n \leqslant 1\), hence \(n = 1\), q.e.d.

Proof of 2.1. The assertion is local on \(X\) and \(Y\) for the étale topology, and one may therefore assume (SGA 1 II 1.1) that \(g\) is the structural morphism of affine space \(\mathbb{E}^m_Y\), and that \(Y\) is affine. Applying the transitivity of local acyclicity 1.13 (i) and the fact that \(\mathbb{E}^m_Y = \mathbb{E}^{m-1}_{\mathbb{E}^1_Y}\), one reduces immediately to the case \(m = 1\), that is, to the case \(X = \operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_Y[t]\).

Let us apply 1.18. One is reduced to proving that the geometric fibres of the morphism of strictly local schemes \(\widetilde{g} : \widetilde{X} \to \widetilde{Y}\), deduced from a pair of geometric points \(\bar{x}\), \(\bar{y}\), where \(\bar{x}\) is closed in the fibre \(X_{\bar{y}}\), are acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\) and \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\). One may obviously assume \(Y = \widetilde{Y}\). Let \(Y' \to Y\) be a finite, local, and surjective morphism, so that \(Y'\) is strictly local, and let \(\bar{y}'\) be the point of \(Y'\) lying over \(\bar{y}\), and \(\bar{x}'\) the point of \(X'\) lying over \(\bar{x}\) and over \(\bar{y}'\). Since \(X' \to X\) is finite, the strict localization of \(X'\) at the point \(\bar{x}'\) is none other than \(\widetilde{X}' = \widetilde{X} \times_Y Y'\). Consequently, every geometric fibre of \(\widetilde{X}'/Y'\) is deduced from a geometric fibre of \(\widetilde{X}/Y\) by an algebraic (necessarily radicial) extension of the base field; moreover there is at least one geometric fibre of \(\widetilde{X}'/Y'\) over each geometric fibre of \(\widetilde{X}/Y\). One may therefore (VIII 1.1) replace \(Y\) by \(Y'\), and by a suitable choice of \(Y'\), one thus reduces to the case where \(k(\bar{x}) = k(\bar{y})\). Then \(\bar{x}\) is a rational point of the fibre \(X_{\bar{y}} = \operatorname{Spec} k(\bar{y})[t]\), say the point \(t = a^o\). Lifting \(a^o\) to a section \(a\) of \(\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{Y}}\) and making the "translation" \(t_1 = t - a\), one reduces to the case where the point \(\bar{x}\) is the point \(\{t = 0\}\) of \(\operatorname{Spec} k(\bar{y})[t]\). Set \(A = \Gamma(\widetilde{Y}, \mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{Y}})\), so that \(A\) is a strictly local ring.

blocks.title: Notation
blocks.html:
Notation 2.3

Let \(A\) be a local henselian ring. One denotes by \(A\{t\}\) the henselization of the ring \(A[t]\) at the prime ideal generated by \(\operatorname{rad} A\) and \(t\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.4

Let \(A\) be henselian and \(A'\) a finite \(A\)-algebra. Then \(A'\{t\} \simeq A' \otimes_A A\{t\}\).
This follows immediately from VIII 4.1. Note that if \(A\) is strictly local, so is \(A\{t\}\).
The proof of the theorem is reduced to the following lemma:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.5

Let \(A\) be a henselian ring of residue characteristic \(p\). Then each geometric fibre of \(\operatorname{Spec} A\{t\}\) over \(\operatorname{Spec} A\) is acyclic and \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L} = \mathbb{P} - \{p\}\).

Note that since \(A\{t\}\) is the henselization of \(A[t]\), a fibre \(\operatorname{Spec} A\{t\} \otimes_A K\), \(K\) a residue field of \(A\), is a projective limit of affine schemes of finite type \(X_i\) over the "line" \(\operatorname{Spec} K[t]\), that is, a limit of affine algebraic curves. Hence each geometric fibre of \(\operatorname{Spec} A\{t\}\) is a limit of affine curves \((X_i)_{\bar{K}}\) over the separably closed field \(\bar{K}\), and it follows from IX 5.7 and VII 5.7 that the cohomological dimension of the geometric fibres is \(\leqslant 1\). It therefore suffices to verify that the geometric fibres are \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\), that is, that such a geometric fibre \(\bar{Z}\) is connected, non-empty, and that \(H^1(\bar{Z},G) = 0\) for each finite \(\mathbb{L}\)-group \(G\).

Let us write \(A = \varinjlim B_\alpha\) where the \(B_\alpha\) are rings of finite type over \(\mathbb{Z}\). The morphism \(B_\alpha \to A\) factors through the henselization \(A_\alpha\) of \(B_\alpha\) at the prime ideal induced by \(\operatorname{rad} A\), whence \(A = \varinjlim A_\alpha\). One readily sees that one also has \(A\{t\} = \varinjlim A_\alpha\{t\}\). Moreover, let \(\bar{y}\) be a geometric point of \(\operatorname{Spec} A\), \(X_{\bar{y}}\) the geometric fibre of \(S = \operatorname{Spec} A\{t\}\) over \(\operatorname{Spec} A\) at \(\bar{y}\), \(\bar{y}_\alpha\) the point of \(\operatorname{Spec} A_\alpha\) induced by \(\bar{y}\), and \(X_{\alpha\,\bar{y}_\alpha}\) the geometric fibre of \(\operatorname{Spec} A_\alpha\{t\}\) over \(\operatorname{Spec} A\) at \(\bar{y}_\alpha\). One has \(X_{\bar{y}} = \varprojlim X_{\alpha\,\bar{y}_\alpha}\). For the proof of 2.5 one is therefore reduced, by 1.7 (ii) (applied to the morphisms \(X_{\alpha\,\bar{y}_\alpha} \to \bar{y}_\alpha\)), to the case \(A = A_\alpha\), that is, where \(A\) is the henselization of an algebra of finite type over \(\mathbb{Z}\) at a given prime ideal. We assume this from now on. Recall that such an algebra is an excellent ring (EGA IV 7.8.3 (iii), 7.8.6 (i)), so that \(A_\alpha\) is likewise excellent (as one sees easily from the definition, cf. EGA IV 18.7.6).

Let us verify \(0\)-acyclicity. (For a more general result, cf. the Appendix.) Since \(A\{t\}/A\) admits the section "\(t = 0\)", a geometric fibre \(\bar{Z}\) is non-empty. To see that it is connected, one is reduced, by replacing \(A\) by a quotient (2.4), to the case where \(A\) is integral and \(\bar{Z}\) is the geometric fibre over the generic point of \(\operatorname{Spec} A\). It suffices to prove that for every finite separable extension \(K'\) of the fraction field \(K\) of \(A\), the scheme \(Z_{K'}\), (\(Z = \operatorname{Spec} A\{t\} \otimes_A K\)) is connected. Let \(A'\) be the normalization of \(A\) in \(K'\) (which is a finite \(A\)-algebra, EGA IV 7.8.2) and \(Z'\) the generic fibre of \(\operatorname{Spec} A'\{t\}\) over \(A'\). By 2.4, one has \(A'\{t\} \simeq A' \otimes_A A\{t\}\), whence \(Z_{K'} \simeq Z'\). Let us replace \(A\) by \(A'\). It then suffices to prove that \(Z\) is integral, and it suffices to prove that \(A\{t\}\) is integral. But \(A\) being normal, \(A[t]\) is, hence \(A\{t\}\) is too (SGA 1 I 9.5 (i)), whence the result.
The proof of 2.5, and consequently of 2.1, is thus reduced to the following lemma, which will be proved in the next section:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.6

Let \(A\) be a henselian and excellent ring, and let \(\bar{Z}\) be a geometric fibre of \(\operatorname{Spec} A\{t\}\) / \(\operatorname{Spec} A\). Then each principal Galois covering \(\bar{Z}'\) of \(\bar{Z}\), of group \(G\) of order prime to the residue characteristic \(p\) of \(A\), is trivial.
3. Proof of the main lemma.

Replacing \(A\) by a finite algebra \(A'\) (cf. 2.4), one reduces assertion 2.6 to the case where \(A\) is integral and \(\bar{Z}\) is the geometric fibre of \(\operatorname{Spec} A\{t\}\) over \(\operatorname{Spec} A\). Let \(K\) be the fraction field of \(A\) and \(Z = \operatorname{Spec} A\{t\} \otimes_A K\). If \(\bar{Z}'/\bar{Z}\) is a principal Galois covering, one may descend it to a \(Z_{K'}\), where \(K'\) is a suitable finite separable extension of \(K\). Replacing (2.4) \(A\) by its normalization in \(K'\), which is a finite \(A\)-algebra (EGA IV 7.8.3 (vi)), one is reduced to proving the lemma in the following form:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.1

With the notation of 2.6, suppose \(A\) normal, and let \(Z'/Z\) be a principal Galois étale covering, of group \(G\) of order prime to the residue characteristic \(p\) of \(A\). Then \(Z'\) is induced by a Galois extension \(K'\) of \(K\), i.e. (SGA 1 IX 6.2) the covering \(\bar{Z}'\) of \(\bar{Z}\) deduced from \(Z'\) is trivial.

Proof. Let \(B'\) be the normalization of \(A\{t\}\) in the ring of rational functions of \(Z'\), and consider the prime ideals \(P\) of height \(1\) of \(A\{t\}\) such that the algebra \(B'\) over \(A\{t\}\) is ramified at \(P\). Since \(Z'/Z\) is étale, \(P\) does not lie over the generic point of \(\operatorname{Spec} A\), i.e., \(\mathfrak{p} = P \cap A \neq 0\). Hence \(A\{t\}/P A\{t\} = (A/\mathfrak{p})\{t\}\) is integral and of dimension at most equal to \(\dim A\). Since \(A\{t\}\) is excellent (EGA IV 7.8.6 (i)) and 18.7.6, hence catenary, one has \(\dim \operatorname{Spec} A\{t\}/P = (\dim A + 1) - 1 = \dim A \geqslant \dim A\{t\}/\mathfrak{p} A\{t\}\), whence \(P = \mathfrak{p} A\{t\}\) since \(P \supset \mathfrak{p} A\{t\}\).

Let \(\mathfrak{p}_1, \ldots, \mathfrak{p}_m\) then be the prime ideals of height \(1\) of \(A\) such that \(B'/A\{t\}\) is ramified at the ideals \(\mathfrak{p}_i A\{t\}\), and let \(s\) be the g.c.d. of the orders of the inertia groups (SGA 2) \(G_i \subset G\) for \(B'\) at the prime ideals lying over the \(\mathfrak{p}_i A\{t\}\), which is an integer dividing the order of \(G\), hence prime to \(p\). Let \(f \in A\) be a function that vanishes to order \(1\) at each \(\mathfrak{p}_i\) (such an \(f\) exists, as follows for example from Bourbaki, Alg. Comm., Chap. II, §3, cor. to prop. 17). Replacing (2.4) \(A\) by its normalization \(A_1\) in the finite extension \(K_1 = K[x]/(x^s - f)\) of \(K\) and \(B'\) by the normalization of \(A_1 \otimes_A B'\), we reduce, by Abhyankar's lemma (SGA 1 X 3.6), to the case where \(B'\) is ramified at no prime ideal of height \(1\) of \(A\{t\}\).

Then the algebra \(B'/A\{t\}\) is also étale over the fibre of \(\operatorname{Spec} A\{t\}\) at every point of \(\operatorname{Spec} A\) of codimension \(1\). Indeed, let \(\mathfrak{p}\) be a prime ideal of height \(1\) of \(A\). Since \(A\) is normal, \(A_{\mathfrak{p}}\) is a discrete valuation ring, hence regular, so \(A\{t\} \otimes_A A_{\mathfrak{p}}\) is also regular — indeed, it is a limit of étale schemes over \(A_{\mathfrak{p}}[t]\). By hypothesis, the algebra \(B'/A\{t\}\) is étale at every point of codimension \(\leqslant 1\) of \(\operatorname{Spec} A\{t\} \otimes_A A_{\mathfrak{p}}\), hence it is étale everywhere by the Zariski-Nagata purity theorem (SGA 1 X 3.1; for a proof, see e.g. SGA 2, X 3.4).

Replacing (2.4) \(A\) by a suitable finite \(A\)-algebra, we reduce to the case where moreover the algebra \(B'/tB'\) over \(A\{t\}/tA\{t\} \simeq A\) is completely decomposed over the generic point of \(\operatorname{Spec} A\). It therefore suffices to prove that, under these conditions, the algebra \(B'\) over \(A\{t\}\) is "trivial"; and since \(A\{t\}\) is henselian, it suffices to prove that \(B'\) over \(A\{t\}\) is étale. Indeed, it follows from the fact that the algebra \(B'/tB'\) splits over the generic point of \(\operatorname{Spec} A\) that it splits over \(\operatorname{Spec}(A)\) (SGA 1 I 10.1), hence that the residue extensions of \(B'\) at the maximal ideal of \(A\{t\}\) are trivial, and we apply (EGA IV 18.5.14). We are thus reduced to the following lemma:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.2

Let \(B\) be an excellent normal local ring, and let \(0 \neq t \in \operatorname{rad} B\) be such that \(B/tB\) is normal. Let \(B'\) be a finite integral normal \(B\)-algebra, containing \(B\), such that:

(i) The algebra \(B'/tB'\) over \(B/tB\) is completely decomposed at the maximal points of \(\operatorname{Spec}(B/tB)\).

(ii) The algebra \(B'\) over \(B\) is étale at the points of codimension \(1\) of \(\operatorname{Spec}(B/tB)\).

Then \(B'\) is étale over \(B\).

Proof. By virtue of (ii), the assertion is trivial for \(\dim B \leqslant 2\), that is, for \(\dim B/tB \leqslant 1\). Suppose that \(B'/B\) is not étale; let \(x\) be a maximal point of the set of points of \(\operatorname{Spec} B/tB\) over which \(B'/B\) is not étale, and let \(C\) be the local ring of \(\operatorname{Spec} B\) at \(x\). Then \(C\) is again an excellent normal ring (EGA IV 7.8.2), we have \(0 \neq t \in \operatorname{rad} C\), and (i) and (ii) hold for the \(C\)-algebra \(C' = C \otimes_B B'\). We may therefore assume \(B = C\), that is, that \(B'\) is étale over \(B\) over every point of \(\operatorname{Spec} B/tB\), except perhaps at the origin. Since \(B/tB\) is normal (in fact unibranch would suffice), condition (i) implies that the algebra \(B'/tB'\) is completely decomposed away from the origin. Moreover, we may assume \(\dim B \geqslant 3\). We are thus reduced to the following lemma:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.3

Let \(B\) be an excellent normal local ring, \(0 \neq t \in \operatorname{rad} B\), \(\dim B \geqslant 3\). Let \(B'\) be a finite normal integral \(B\)-algebra, containing \(B\), such that the algebra \(B'/tB'\) over \(B/tB\) is completely decomposed away from the origin. Then \(B'\) is étale over \(B\).

Proof. Let \(X = \operatorname{Spec} B\), \(X_1 = X - \{x_o\}\), where \(x_o\) is the closed point, and let \(i : U \to X\) be the open set of those \(x \in X\) at which the algebra \(B'/B\) is étale. Then \((X - U) \cap V(t) = \{x_o\}\) has dimension \(0\). Since \(V(t)\) is defined by a single equation, it follows that \(\dim(X - U) \leqslant 1\) (EGA \(0_{\mathrm{IV}}\) 16.2.5), hence (\(X\) being catenary) \(x \in X - U \Longrightarrow \dim \mathcal{O}_{X,x} \geqslant \dim B - 1 \geqslant 2\), i.e. \(\operatorname{codim}(X - U, X) \geqslant 2\).

Let \(X' = \operatorname{Spec}(B')\), and let \(U'\) be the inverse image of \(U\) in \(X'\); then, \(X\) being universally catenary, the relation \(\operatorname{codim}(X - U, X) \geqslant 2\) implies the relation \(\operatorname{codim}(X' - U', X') \geqslant 2\) (EGA IV 5.6.10), hence, \(X'\) being normal, we have
\[B' = \Gamma(X', \mathcal{O}_{X'}) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \Gamma(U', \mathcal{O}_{U'}) \;.\]

Let then \(\underline{B}' = \widetilde{B}'\) be the sheaf of \(\mathcal{O}_X\)-algebras defining \(X'\) over \(X\), and \(\underline{C}\) its restriction to \(U\); then the preceding formula is equivalent to the formula
\[\underline{B}' \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } i_*(\underline{C}) \;,\]

and 3.3 thus reduces to the following statement (in which \(B'\) no longer figures): Let \(B\), \(t\) be as in 3.3, \(X = \operatorname{Spec}(B)\), \(Y = \operatorname{Spec}(B/tB)\), \(U\) an open neighbourhood of \(Y_1 = Y - \{x_o\}\) in \(X_1 = X - \{x_o\}\), \(U'\) an étale covering of \(U\) whose restriction to \(Y_1\) is completely decomposed, \(\underline{C}\) the sheaf of \(\mathcal{O}_{U'}\)-algebras defining \(U'\); then (\(i : U \to X\) denoting the canonical immersion) \(i_*(\underline{C})\) is a coherent étale Algebra over \(X\) (or, what amounts to the same, by virtue of the relation \(\operatorname{prof} \mathcal{O}_{X,x} \geqslant 2\) for \(x \in X - U\) noted above and of EGA IV 5.10.5, \(U'\) extends to an étale covering \(X'\) of \(X\)).

Let \(\widehat{X} = \operatorname{Spec} \widehat{B}\), where \(\widehat{B}\) is the completion of \(B\). Then \(\widehat{B}\) is normal (EGA IV 7.8.3 (v)) and \(\widehat{B}/B\) is faithfully flat. Let
\[\xymatrix{ \widehat{U} \ar[r]^{\widehat{i}} \ar[d]_{f_1} & \widehat{X} \ar[d]^{f} \\ U \ar[r]_{i} & X }\]

the cartesian diagram deduced from \(\widehat{X} \to X\). Since \(f\) is faithfully flat, the functor \(i_*\) commutes with the base change \(f\) (EGA IV 2.3.1), and we are reduced (EGA IV 17.7.1) to proving that \(\widehat{i}_*(\widehat{\underline{C}})\) is an étale algebra over \(\widehat{X}\). We may therefore replace \(B\) by \(\widehat{B}\), that is, we may assume \(B\) complete. In this case, we shall prove that \(U'\) is a completely decomposed covering of \(U\) (which will obviously imply that it extends to an étale covering of \(X\), and will complete the proof). Now this assertion is now an immediate consequence of the "local Lefschetz theory" SGA 2 X 2.1 (i) and 2.5, as one sees at once, taking into account once again the relation \(\operatorname{prof} \mathcal{O}_{X,x} \geqslant 2\) for \(\dim \{x\} = 1\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.4

One can prove 3.2 and 3.3 under more general conditions, following essentially the same proof: instead of assuming \(B\) excellent and normal, it suffices to assume that the completion \(\widehat{B}\) is normal (a condition which is stable under localization, by virtue of the results of EGA IV 7), or only that the completion of \(B\) for the \((tB)\)-adic topology is normal, and a quotient of a regular ring.
4. Appendix: A criterion for local \(0\)-acyclicity.
The results of the present section will no longer be used in the remainder of the seminar.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 4.1

Let \(g : X \to Y\) be a morphism of schemes. Suppose \(g\) is flat with separable fibres, and that \(X\) and \(Y\) are locally noetherian, resp. that \(g\) is locally of finite presentation. Then \(g\) is universally locally \(0\)-acyclic.

We may obviously assume \(X\) and \(Y\) affine, which allows us, in the resp. case, to reduce to the case where \(Y\), hence \(X\), is noetherian, by the standard method of EGA IV 8, using here EGA IV 9.7.7. We may therefore confine ourselves to proving the first statement. The hypothesis being stable under base change of finite type, we are reduced, taking into account the passage to the limit 1.13 (ii), to proving that \(g\) is locally \(0\)-acyclic; and for this we are reduced by 1.17 to proving that if we assume moreover that \(g\) is strictly local, then the geometric fibres of \(g\) are connected. But this is precisely what EGA IV 18.9.8 states.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.2

Let \(g : X \to Y\) be a morphism of schemes, with \(Y\) discrete. Then \(g\) is universally locally \(0\)-acyclic.

We may assume that \(Y\) is the spectrum of a perfect field \(k\) (VIII 1.1). On the other hand, we may assume \(X\) affine, hence a projective limit of affine schemes of finite type over \(k\), and taking 1.13 (ii) into account we are reduced to the case where \(X\) is of finite type over \(k\). Finally, we may obviously assume \(X\) reduced, hence separable over \(k\) since \(k\) is perfect. The conclusion then follows from 4.1.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.3

Suppose that \(g\) is surjective and satisfies the conditions of 4.1 or of 4.2; in the non-resp. case of 4.1 suppose moreover that \(g\) is either quasi-compact and quasi-separated, or universally open. Then \(g\) is a morphism of universal effective descent for the fibred category of étale sheaves on variable preschemes.

In the cases under consideration, \(g\) is universally submersive, and it follows from VIII 9.4 that \(g\) is a morphism of universal descent for the fibred category in question. This allows us, for the question of effectivity, to confine ourselves to the case \(Y\) affine. Moreover, one sees, in each of the cases under consideration, that \(X\) is covered by a finite number of affine open sets \(X_i\) whose images cover \(Y\). Replacing \(X\) by the disjoint sum of the \(X_i\), we may then assume \(X\) affine, a fortiori quasi-compact and quasi-separated over \(Y\). We then conclude by the argument of VIII 9.4.1, using the fact XVI 1.1 that, for a quasi-compact and quasi-separated morphism \(g\), the formation of \(g_*(F)\) (\(F\) an étale sheaf on \(X\)) commutes with every base change \(Y' \to Y\) that is locally \(0\)-acyclic.

blocks.title: Remarks
blocks.html:
Remarks 4.4

a) One thus obtains the proof (which had been left in abeyance) of VIII 9.4 d), as a special case of 4.3. A different, easier proof, not using the rather delicate result of EGA IV 18.9.8, would be obtained by noting that, thanks to VIII 9.1, one may confine oneself to the case of the morphism \(\operatorname{Spec}(K) \to \operatorname{Spec}(k)\) induced by a field extension \(K/k\); now \(\operatorname{Spec}(K)\) is universally locally \(0\)-acyclic over \(\operatorname{Spec}(k)\), for it is even universally acyclic for \(\mathbb{L} = \mathbb{P} - \{p\}\), \(p = \operatorname{car} k\), as will be seen in XVI 1.5.

b) It is not known whether every quasi-compact and quasi-separated morphism that is surjective and locally \((-1)\)-acyclic (or universally locally \((-1)\)-acyclic) is a morphism of effective descent for the fibred category of étale sheaves on variable preschemes. This statement seems fairly plausible, and would improve 4.3 and VIII 9.4 c), d). It should be compared with the effectivity statement in MURRE, Sém. Bourbaki no. 293, p. 17.

c) It is plausible that, under the conditions of 4.2, \(g\) is even locally acyclic for \(\mathbb{L}\) and locally \(1\)-aspherical for \(\mathbb{L}\), where \(\mathbb{L}\) is the set of prime numbers distinct from the residue characteristics of \(Y\). In this question one may obviously assume \(Y\) to be the spectrum of an algebraically closed field \(k\), and one can show (SGA 1964/65) that the answer is affirmative when one has resolution of singularities for schemes of finite type over \(k\). Hence the answer is affirmative when \(Y\) is of characteristic zero, as one sees using the results of HIRONAKA (∗).
